entities.name: Treaty of Jassy
entities.label: Text
entities.summary:
The Treaty of Jassy, signed on January 9, 1792, marked a pivotal moment in Eastern European history, concluding the Russo-Turkish War (1787–1792) and establishing a new balance of power in the region. This treaty was significant not only for the Russian Empire, led by Tsarina Catherine the Great, but also for the Ottoman Empire, which faced territorial losses and a shift in influence. The geographic scope of the treaty extended across the Black Sea region, notably affecting territories such as Moldavia and Wallachia, and it set the stage for future conflicts and diplomatic relations in Europe.

Key events leading to the Treaty of Jassy included a series of military engagements, culminating in the decisive Russian victory at the Battle of Rymnik in 1789. The treaty formalized the territorial agreements that had been reached through these military campaigns, resulting in the recognition of Russian suzerainty over Moldavia and Wallachia while also affirming the independence of the Crimean Khanate from Ottoman control. This agreement effectively reduced Ottoman influence in Eastern Europe and signaled the rising power of Russia as a dominant force on the continent.

The legacy of the Treaty of Jassy reverberated through the 19th century, as it laid the groundwork for further Russian expansion into the Balkans and influenced the complex web of alliances that characterized European politics. The treaty's stipulations regarding territorial changes and political autonomy set a precedent for future treaties and conflicts, ultimately contributing to the disintegration of Ottoman authority in Europe. As historian Mark Mazower remarked, 'The borders drawn at Jassy would echo in the political landscape of Europe long after the treaty was signed.'
